title: Swedish winter bird communities did not follow year-to-year temperature more than summer communities on the same routes in 1975-2024; waterbirds and the prior winter gave most of the winter response
abstract: Question: do winter bird communities follow temperature in time more closely than breeding communities, and is the winter response short-term redistribution or a lasting change? Data: Swedish Bird Survey winter point-count routes (16,767 Christmas counts on 2,350 routes, winters 1975/76-2023/24, up to five counts per winter, snow cover from 1991) and summer point-count routes (11,011 counts, 1,256 routes); 506 routes have both; same observer per route; E-OBS temperature; European species temperature indices from GBIF winter and June records. Method: community temperature index (CTI) slopes as fractions of the spatial CTI-temperature slope, route fixed effects, two-way route x season bootstrap, species-shuffle nulls, snow and count-day temperature covariates, a placebo with temperature after the count. Results: the winter CTI followed 4.9% (2.7-7.5%) of the spatial slope from year to year and the summer CTI 3.6-6.8%; the paired winter-minus-summer difference was -0.5 points (-7.2 to 5.7). The winter slope did not exceed a species-shuffle null (p = 0.25); the summer slope did (p = 0.04). Waterbirds gave most of the winter response; without them the fraction was 2.2% (-0.2 to 4.5%). Within one winter the fraction was 6.5% and fell to 3.8% with snow cover; full snow lowered the CTI as much as 0.28 C on the spatial gradient. The previous winter raised the CTI as much as the current weeks (0.0054 versus 0.0059 C per C), also without waterbirds; wren, blackbird, goldcrest, grey heron and green woodpecker gave this carry-over. The winter CTI rose 2.7 times faster than the summer CTI, but winters also warmed faster, and per degree the slow fractions did not clearly differ. Limitations: the fast response is national-scale and vanishes with season fixed effects; volunteer-chosen routes; no ice data; the two slow estimators disagree in sign.
